title: Resolving questions, II
research_question: How should a formal semantics distinguish questions, propositions, and facts while explaining the shared semantic relations that allow facts to resolve questions and prove propositions?
methodology: The accessible abstract describes a formal, situation-semantics analysis rather than an empirical experiment. Part II motivates an ontology in which propositions, questions, and facts are distinct semantic objects while formal relations connect facts to both propositions and questions. The analysis is then used to account for factivity with predicates such as know and for the behavior of adverbially modified predicates with interrogative, declarative, and fact-nominal arguments.

key_findings.finding: The paper argues for an ontology that distinguishes propositions, questions, and facts instead of reducing these categories to a single type of semantic object.
Despite this ontological distinction, the analysis identifies a common role for facts: facts can prove propositions and resolve questions.
The proposed relation between facts and propositions/questions is used to explain why predicates such as know carry factive presuppositions.
The framework is also applied to the behavior of adverbially modified predicates when their arguments are interrogatives, declaratives, or fact-denoting nominals.

In the broader two-part theory summarized by the abstract, a question is not reductively identified with its answers, allowing question resolution to depend on contextual parameters such as conversational goals and inferential capabilities.

limitations: Only the abstract and bibliographic record were accessible through a reliable correctly identified source, so the detailed formal derivations, linguistic examples, objections, and scope conditions of Part II could not be independently assessed.
The accessible material reports a theoretical semantic analysis rather than a quantitative empirical evaluation, and it provides no dataset, experimental metrics, or reproducibility artifact.
Because full text was unavailable in the source used for analysis, claims beyond those explicitly summarized in the abstract were not inferred.
raw_claims: The theory is formulated within a situation-semantics framework.
Questions are treated as semantic objects distinct from propositions and facts.
The analysis does not reduce questions simply to collections of their answers.
Facts are related to propositions through a proof relation.
Facts are related to questions through a resolution relation.
The common semantic role of facts is used in the analysis of factive predicates such as know.
The framework addresses predicates that combine with interrogative, declarative, and fact-nominal arguments.
The broader theory makes whether an answer resolves a question sensitive to contextual factors such as goals and inferential capabilities.
